statement.p:
We'll begin with a set of three data points
\dvec_1=\twovec11, \hspace{24pt} \dvec_2=\twovec21, \hspace{24pt} \dvec_3=\twovec34.
Find the centroid, or mean, \overline{\dvec} = \frac1N\sum_j \dvec_j. Then plot the data points and their centroid in .
Plot the data points and their centroid here.
A standard coordinate grid and set of axes.
A standard 1\times1 coordinate grid and set of axes. The horizontal and vertical ranges run from -4 to 4.
Notice that the centroid lies in the center of the data so the spread of the data will be measured by how far away the points are from the centroid. To simplify our calculations, find the demeaned data points
\dtil_j = \dvec_j - \overline{\dvec}
and plot them in .
Plot the demeaned data points \dtil_j here.
A standard coordinate grid and set of axes.
A standard 1\times1 coordinate grid and set of axes. The horizontal and vertical ranges run from -4 to 4.
Now that the data has been demeaned, we will define the total variance as the average of the squares of the distances from the origin; that is, the total variance is
V = \frac 1N\sum_j~|\dtil_j|^2.
Find the total variance V for our set of three points.
Now plot the projections of the demeaned data onto the x and y axes using and find the variances V_x and V_y of the projected points.
Plot the projections of the demeaned data onto the x and y axes.
A horizontal number line.
A horizontal number line beginning on the left at -4 and ending on the right at 4.
A vertical number line
A vertical number line beginning on the bottom at -4 and ending on the top at 4.
Which of the variances, V_x and V_y, is larger and how does the plot of the projected points explain your response?
What do you notice about the relationship between V, V_x, and V_y? How does the Pythagorean theorem explain this relationship?
Plot the projections of the demeaned data points onto the lines defined by vectors \vvec_1=\twovec11 and \vvec_2=\twovec{-1}1 using and find the variances V_{\vvec_1} and V_{\vvec_2} of these projected points.
Plot the projections of the deameaned data onto the lines defined by \vvec_1 and \vvec_2.
A coordinate grid and set of axes along with two orthogonal lines at 45 degrees to the axes.
A standard 1\times1 coordinate grid, a set of axes, and two orthogonal lines parallel to the vectors \vvec_1=\twovec11 and \vvec_2=\twovec{-1}1.
What is the relationship between the total variance V and V_{\vvec_1} and V_{\vvec_2}? How does the Pythagorean theorem explain your response?

li.p: We find V_x = 2/3 and V_y=2. Notice that V_y is larger because the points are more spread out in the vertical direction.
We have V=V_x+V_y due to the Pythagorean theorem.
The points projected onto the line defined by \vvec_1 are \twovec{-1}{-1}, \twovec{-1/2}{-1/2}, and \twovec{3/2}{3/2}. This gives the variance V_{\vvec_1} = 7/3.
The points projected onto the line defined by \vvec_2 are \twovec{0}{0}, \twovec{1/2}{-1/2}, and \twovec{-1/2}{1/2}. This gives the variance V_{\vvec_2} = 1/3.
Once again, V = V_{\vvec_1} + V_{\vvec_2} because of the Pythagorean theorem.
